claims.text: The initial FeCoNi-based alloy is single-phase fcc.
The initial alloy has coercivity below 100 Oe.
The initial alloy has high saturation magnetization.
A controlled thermal-aging treatment can induce fine nanoscale precipitates within the fcc matrix.
Aging at approximately 600–700 °C for 3–6 hours followed by rapid quenching is an appropriate treatment window.
Thermal aging will produce nanometer-sized secondary precipitates or early-stage spinodal-decomposition features.
Thermal aging induces phase separation within the fcc matrix.
The phase separation produces hard-magnetic precipitates.
The precipitates create local regions of high magnetocrystalline anisotropy.
The precipitates act as domain-wall pinning centers.
Domain-wall pinning impedes wall motion under an applied magnetic field and increases coercivity.
The aged alloy will have higher coercivity than the matched single-phase fcc baseline.
The aged alloy's coercivity will rise significantly above 100 Oe.
The coercivity increase could be a doubling or more after optimization.
Controlled precipitation can enhance coercivity without unacceptably reducing saturation magnetization.

contradictions.description: The main prediction requires coercivity significantly above 100 Oe and suggests a possible doubling, whereas the falsification rule only rejects an increase below 50%. An increase of at least 50% that remains at or below 100 Oe would fail the principal predicted outcome but would not falsify the hypothesis under the stated rule.
